name: Luddites
info: The Luddites were English textile workers who, between 1811 and 1816, broke machines in organised raids in the Midlands, Yorkshire and the North West, protesting over pay, working conditions, child labour and the quality of output.

facts.where: England: Nottinghamshire and the Midlands, beginning at Arnold near Nottingham; the West Riding of Yorkshire, around Huddersfield, Marsden and Cleckheaton; Lancashire and the North West, at Middleton and Westhoughton; Loughborough in 1816
facts.period: begins at Arnold, 11 March 1811; Nottinghamshire from November 1811; the West Riding in early 1812; Lancashire; the York trial, January 1813; last raids in 1816; the Pentrich Rising of 1817, sometimes seen as the last major Luddite act
facts.figures: “Ned Ludd”, the legendary weaver or apprentice whose name signed their letters; George Mellor, who led the killing of the mill owner William Horsfall; Jeremiah Brandreth, a probable ex-Luddite who led the Pentrich Rising; Lord Byron, their defender in the House of Lords
facts.outcome: suppressed by 12,000 troops, a law making machine-breaking a capital crime and the York trials, whose sentences of execution and transportation quickly ended the movement; the name later came to mean anyone opposed to new technology

t: The Luddites were not opposed to machines as such, and many were skilled machine operators; they attacked the machines of manufacturers who were circumventing the standard labour practices of the time.
Each region wrecked the machines that threatened its own trade: wide knitting frames in the Midlands, steam-powered looms in the North West, and shearing frames and gig mills in Yorkshire.
The government answered with 12,000 troops, made machine-breaking a capital crime in 1812 and staged a mass trial at York in 1813, whose executions and transportations quickly ended the movement.
dyk: The Yorkshire croppers broke the cropping machines made by Enoch Taylor of Marsden with a hammer they called “Enoch”, purportedly shouting, “Enoch made them, and Enoch shall break them.”

sections.background:
In the 18th century the “domestic” manufacturers were notorious for precarious work. Underemployment was chronic, and it was common to keep a larger workforce than needed as insurance against labour shortages in boom times. The organisation of the textile industry by merchant capitalists was inherently unstable: with their capital still largely in raw materials, they could easily take on work when trade was good and cut back when it was bad, and they lacked the later factory owners’ interest in a steady rate of production. Seasonal swings in wages and violent short-term fluctuations caused by harvests and war produced periodic outbreaks of violence.

Machine-breaking had a long history, especially in the hosiery and woollen trades. Stockingers had taken organised action at various times since 1675, and new cotton-spinning technologies in Lancashire, which could be worked by less-skilled, low-wage labourers, met violent resistance in 1768 and 1779. Parliament answered with acts such as the Protection of Stocking Frames, etc. Act 1788. Rising food prices caused riots too, among the Keelmen on the Tyne in 1710 and the tin miners at Falmouth in 1727.

The Luddite movement itself emerged in the harsh economic climate of the Napoleonic Wars. The British economy suffered greatly from 1810 to 1812, with high unemployment and inflation, caused by the cost of the wars with Napoleon, his Continental System of economic warfare and an escalating conflict with the United States.
sections.aims:
The Luddites protested against certain types of automated machinery because of their concerns over workers’ pay, labour savings, child labour, working conditions and the quality of output. They were not opposed to machines as such, and many were skilled operators in the textile industry; they attacked manufacturers who were trying to circumvent the standard labour practices of the time. Each region wrecked the machinery that threatened its own trade: in the Midlands the “wide” knitting frames used to make cheap and inferior lace articles, in the North West the steam-powered looms that threatened wages in the cotton trade, and in Yorkshire the shearing frames and gig mills used to finish woollen cloth.

Many Luddite groups were highly organised and used machine-breaking as one of several tools for specific political ends. Their letters to industrialists and officials explained why they destroyed machinery and threatened more if the “obnoxious” machines stayed in use. The Midlands Luddites appealed to the legitimacy of the Company of Framework Knitters; in the North West, which lacked such institutions, letters sought recognition as a united body of tradespeople, asked for higher minimum wages and an end to child labour, and used radical language linking the movement to the American and French revolutionaries.

The historian Malcolm I. Thomis argued that the attacks implied no hostility to machinery as such, and Eric Hobsbawm called them “collective bargaining by riot”.
sections.events:
The movement began at Arnold, Nottinghamshire, on 11 March 1811 and spread rapidly through England over the next two years. Its main areas of operation were Nottinghamshire from November 1811, the West Riding of Yorkshire from early 1812, and then Lancashire. Luddites met at night on the moors around the industrial towns to practise military-like drills and manoeuvres, and besides their raids they organised public demonstrations and sent letters to industrialists and officials. In Yorkshire the letters turned to more violent threats against local authorities.

Luddites clashed with government troops at Burton’s Mill in Middleton and at Westhoughton Mill, both in Lancashire, and mill and factory owners took to shooting protesters. Four Luddites led by George Mellor ambushed and killed the mill owner William Horsfall of Ottiwells Mill in Marsden at Crosland Moor in Huddersfield; Horsfall had said that he would “ride up to his saddle in Luddite blood”. The Luddites and their supporters sent anonymous death threats to magistrates and food merchants, and may have attacked some.

After an attack on Cartwright’s Mill at Rawfolds near Cleckheaton, the government staged a mass trial at York in January 1813. Activists still smashed Heathcote’s lace-making machine in Loughborough in 1816, and he and other industrialists built secret chambers in their buildings to hide in during an attack. In 1817 Jeremiah Brandreth led the Pentrich Rising, a general uprising unrelated to machinery that can be seen as the last major Luddite act.
sections.people:
The Luddites called themselves followers of “Ned Ludd”, a legendary weaver whose name was used as a pseudonym in threatening letters to mill owners and government officials; the name occurs in their writings as early as 1811. Ned Ludd was said to be an apprentice who smashed two stocking frames in 1779 after being criticised and told to change his method. He often appears as Captain, General or King Ludd, and the legends place his home either in Anstey, near Leicester, or in Sherwood Forest.

Most Luddites were textile workers, many of them skilled. In Yorkshire the croppers, who faced mass unemployment when Enoch Taylor of Marsden introduced cropping machines, broke the machines with a hammer they called “Enoch” to mock him. George Mellor fired the shot that killed William Horsfall; of the four men arrested, Benjamin Walker turned informant and the other three were hanged. Jeremiah Brandreth, who led the Pentrich Rising of 1817, was an unemployed Nottingham stockinger and probably a former Luddite.

Lord Byron was one of the few prominent defenders of the Luddites. In the House of Lords on 27 February 1812 he denounced the plight of the working class and the government’s ruthless repression, saying he had never, even in the most oppressed provinces of Turkey, seen “such squalid wretchedness” as in the heart of a Christian country, and he opposed the law that made machine-breaking a capital crime.
sections.outcomes:
The Luddites won none of their demands. The crisis of 1810 to 1812 led to widespread protest and violence, but the middle and upper classes strongly supported the government, which used the army to suppress all working-class unrest, and the Luddites above all. Some 12,000 government troops, most of them militia or yeomanry, were involved, a larger number, Eric Hobsbawm wrote, than the army the Duke of Wellington led into Portugal in 1808 during the Peninsular War.

Parliament made machine-breaking a capital crime with the Destruction of Stocking Frames, etc. Act 1812. At the mass trial at York in January 1813 the government charged over 60 men, among them Mellor and his companions, with crimes connected with Luddism. Some were Luddites, but many had no connection to the movement. The proceedings were legitimate jury trials, yet many cases were abandoned for lack of evidence and 30 men were acquitted. The trials were meant as show trials to deter others, and the harsh sentences of those found guilty, which included execution and penal transportation, quickly ended the movement.

Historians have explained the tactic in different ways. Thomis saw machine-breaking as one of the very few tactics that workers had to put pressure on employers, undermine lower-paid rivals and build solidarity. Hobsbawm explained it as a tactic used in Britain since the Restoration, because manufactories were scattered across the country and large-scale strikes were impractical.
sections.legacy:
Machine-breaking did not end with the Luddites. An agricultural variant of Luddism occurred in the widespread Swing Riots of 1830 in southern and eastern England, which centred on breaking threshing machines. The Luddites are remembered in the Yorkshire folk song “The Cropper Lads”, recorded by Lou Killen and Maddy Prior among others, and in the traditional song “The Triumph of General Ludd”, which Chumbawamba recorded for their 1988 album English Rebel Songs.

Their name took on a life of its own. Today “Luddite” is sometimes used for anyone who opposes or resists new technologies. In a British parliamentary debate in 1956 a Labour spokesman said that organised workers were by no means wedded to a “Luddite Philosophy”. By 2006 the term neo-Luddism had emerged for opposition to many forms of technology; a manifesto of the Second Luddite Congress, held at Barnesville, Ohio, in April 1996, called it “a leaderless movement of passive resistance to consumerism and the increasingly bizarre and frightening technologies of the Computer Age”.

Economists speak of the “Luddite fallacy”, the fear that technological unemployment must cause lasting structural unemployment. Through the 20th century and the first decade of the 21st the dominant view among economists was that it was indeed a fallacy, but more recently there has been growing support for the view that the benefits of automation are not equally shared.

summary: The Luddites were English textile workers who broke machines in organised raids between 1811 and 1816, in the Midlands, Yorkshire and the North West, over pay, conditions and the quality of work. Troops, a law making machine-breaking a capital crime and the York trials of 1813 suppressed them, and their name came to mean any opponent of new technology.

notes: Dates: the lede gives 1811–1816; the section heading says “Peak activity: 1811–1817” and calls the 1817 Pentrich Rising the last major Luddite act. I used end 1816 and kept Pentrich as an event; 1817 would also be defensible.
The article gives two starts: “began in Arnold, Nottinghamshire, on 11 March 1811” and “main areas of operation began in Nottinghamshire in November 1811”. I gave both.

The article says Lancashire followed “by March 1813”, after the York trial of January 1813; that looks wrong (the Middleton and Westhoughton clashes are not dated in the article). I wrote only “and then Lancashire” and did not date the Lancashire clashes.
The killing of Horsfall is not dated in the article, so it is undated here; the York trial is placed after the Rawfolds attack as the article has it.
The article’s lede calls Ned Ludd “a legendary weaver”; the etymology section “an apocryphal apprentice”. I gave both.
Left out the Northumberland and Durham rebellion of 1740 and the assault on Quaker corn dealers of 1756 for length.
The article is thin; the outcomes and legacy sections lean on the historians’ views and modern usage, as the article gives them.
